name: NATO: an allied tactical air force (composite)
description: A superior air force: a daily air tasking order, packages built around strike flights with suppression, stand-off jamming, decoys and escorts, a long and methodical campaign to roll back the air defences, then interdiction and support of the land battle. Strong ELINT, satellites and reconnaissance; coalition politics, a low tolerance for losses and prisoners, and anti-radiation missiles in short supply.
source: usaf_ato_doctrine and wiki_ato (the daily tasking order and its cycle); jsead_1982 and jp3_01_4_1995 (SEAD: campaign, localized and opportune suppression); afmag_1989_slam (hunter-killer teams, the three ways of jamming, HARM in short supply); decoys (decoy drones before the strike, the Bekaa 1982); every number not named there is a game value
notes: Composite and fictional: the units are not real NATO units. Aircraft types are period types named for flavour; every aircraft number is a PLACEHOLDER (docs/air_war/01_FACTIONS.md).

comms_jamming.name: the ground jamming group (TACJAM)
comms_jamming.source: palii_1989 pp. 22-23 (a group of 15-18 ground jammers of 1-2 kW against HF and VHF links out to 30 km into the tactical depth; the AN/MLQ-34 TACJAM 20-150 MHz; troop air defence among the first targets); dtic_quickfix_tacjam (TACJAM before its production decision in 1979); follow_s and standing at the line are sam3d readings
comms_jamming.notes: The Soviet reading of NATO's jammers (docs/research/VOICE_JAMMING_2026-10.md section 1); its fielding in Europe by 1985 is not confirmed. Power taken in the middle of Palii's 1-2 kW. No period source gives how fast a spot jammer finds a spare frequency (section 3.4).

comms_jamming.name: Quick Fix (EH-1H/EH-60A)
comms_jamming.source: palii_1989 p. 23 (the AN/ALQ-151 Quick Fix: 2-76 MHz, out to 60 km); dtic_quickfix_tacjam (the EH-1H with the AN/ARQ-33 in airworthiness tests in 1977); its orbit 5 km behind its own line and follow_s are sam3d readings
comms_jamming.notes: No source gives its transmitter's power, so within its range it jams weak, never strong (air_war/comms_jamming.hpp). In 1985 most likely the EH-1H (docs/research/VOICE_JAMMING_2026-10.md section 1.1).

phases.name: counter-air and suppression, with interdiction from the first day
phases.notes: Until the intelligence believes fewer than 45% of the air defences still work. Interdiction and support from the first day at a reduced share (roadmap B11, docs/air_battle/10_FACTIONS.md section 9.2): the Bekaa's suppress-then-strike in the same raid (lambeth_1984), JSEAD doctrine by 1982 (jsead_1982); that NATO in 1985 would fly both from day 1 a SAM3D inference (factions_cases.md section 1); the shares game values. apportion_mode0: the shares a save made before it keeps.

armed_recce.notes: Armed reconnaissance of the supply roads and railways: pairs searching a stretch behind the line and attacking what they find (the follow-on forces attack, adopted November 1984: wiki_fofa).

strike.notes: Strike flights with hunter-killer SEAD, an EF-111A standing off, escort against the defender's fighters (afmag_1989_slam). medium_below_iads: medium altitude only once the believed working defences are below the rollback's line (roadmap B11, docs/air_battle/10_FACTIONS.md section 9.1: rafhs_j20_1999, mt_1984_babich; the line a game value).

dead.notes: Decoys first to make the site radiate, ARMs on what radiates, bombs on the located site (the Bekaa: decoys).

hunter.notes: A hunter-killer team on patrol over a suspected battery: fires on whatever radiates (opportune suppression: jp3_01_4_1995).

deception.notes: A wave of decoy drones to drain the battery's missiles and make it radiate for the ELINT.

missile.notes: Cruise missile salvos at fixed targets deep or heavily defended, without a crew at risk: only in a war of 1986 or later (TLAM-C from ships, then the B-52s' AGM-86C); in the 1980-85 war NATO has none.

intelligence.source: vr_1985_plss (stand-off TDOA location of a new emitter within seconds: elint_k_m, elint_delay_h); afmag_2000_kosovo (inflated claims, design reference only: bda_overclaim); satellite passes and latencies are game values (a period source on pass warning is an open item: docs/research/ENEMY_AIR_RESEARCH_2026-10.md section 7)

logistics.notes: buildup: an allied air force deploys into the theatre: GWAPS's Phase I (16 squadrons from the US and 4 from Europe) was complete within four weeks (gwaps_vol3 pp. 298-299); Allied Force began with 430 aircraft and asked for nearly 1,000 after three weeks (rand_mr1365 p. 33)
logistics.source: afmag_1989_slam (HARM in short supply, Shrike older: a stock the rollback spends in two or three days); the numbers are game values (balance pass, docs/air_war/09_BALANCE.md)

close_support.source: fm_100_5_1982 p. 7-11 (close air support and battlefield air interdiction of the attack, BAI against targets positioned to directly affect friendly forces either side of the FSCL; the ground commander must suppress the enemy's air defences for it: the risk gates); fm_101_5_1_1980 pp. 1-15, 1-16. The worth itself is a game value: one axis of its own believed advancing (attacking at commanders.moving_km_per_day or faster in its own picture) is worth a troops target of value 0.5 at weight 1, above the reward gate (min_reward 0.3, at most 0.36 with an unambitious chief), so the axis alone is reason enough to step; the risk gates still decide

air_front.source: SAM3D estimates bounded by the cases (docs/research/fronts_2026-11/air_ground_cases.md section 7): the superior faction opens a sector when the believed working fire units over a 20 km strip fall to 30% of their pre-war number (brant_1986_bai_1973 ch. 4, a SAM-free corridor about 24 km wide; werrell_2005 p. 153, full close support under 24 h from the first sites destroyed: the delay); pulls back above 2% lost a sortie (jvl_1973_losses, werrell_2005 pp. 151, 154: the normal 1973 rate just over 1%, the IAF's 4% that stopped it); 60 km greatest depth; a crisis on its own ground front lets it ignore the loss gate for 1-3 days (entwistle_1988 ch. 4-5, the Golan). min_reward is a game value
air_front.notes: docs/fronts/02_AIR_FRONT.md section 3. The chief's traits move the gates by at most air_front.trait_shift of their value; the gates never open in a sector no band of which was ever believed covered (air_front.min_baseline).

politics.source: nmusaf_sanctuaries (no-strike zones and target approval from above); hgram_080 (higher authority setting the time on target: interference_per_cycle); the numbers are game values. The nation's infrastructure kinds (refinery to exchange, 22 Oct 2026) are game values by analogy; a kind of the power grid (substation, dam) is banned wherever power_plant is. The escalation event unbans the whole grid

officers.name: Thomas R. Halloran
officers.background: USAF fighter pilot, two tours over North Vietnam, staff of Allied Air Forces Central Europe
officers.bio: Learned in Route Package Six what flying into an air defence without suppression costs. Patient, political, ambitious for his fourth star.

officers.name: Dieter Kessler
officers.background: Luftwaffe Tornado navigator, instructor on NATO's Tactical Leadership Programme
officers.bio: Plays chess against the air defence. Never comes the same way twice; likes to make the radars look the wrong way first.

officers.name: Alistair Pryce
officers.bio: Trusts a photograph, distrusts a pilot. Wants fresh imagery of anything that moves before it is struck.

officers.name: Raymond Duquesne
officers.background: F-4G electronic warfare officer, then pilot
officers.bio: Counts every HARM as if it were his last, because in this war it might be.

officers.name: Earl Becker
officers.bio: First in, last out. Takes it personally when a battery kills one of his.

officers.name: Gianni Ferraro
officers.bio: Believes the night and the valleys are a Tornado's best armour.
